metadata.documentTitle: NDMA Guidelines on Building Collapse Emergency Response
metadata.cleanText: For building collapse rescue: (1) Establish a safety perimeter around the collapse zone. (2) Shut off gas and electricity supply to the area. (3) Conduct rapid visual assessment and listen for survivors. (4) Use trained search dogs and electronic listening devices to locate trapped persons. (5) Begin rescue from the edges of the debris pile, working inward. (6) Use cribbing and shoring techniques to stabilize debris before removing it. (7) Protect survivors from secondary collapse using temporary supports. (8) Deploy heavy equipment only after confirming no survivors are in the immediate removal area. (9) Maintain continuous communication with trapped survivors to monitor their condition.

metadata.documentTitle: NDMA Guidelines on Building Collapse Emergency Response
metadata.cleanText: Medical considerations for collapse victims: (1) Crush syndrome is a major risk for persons trapped under heavy debris for extended periods. (2) Before extracting a crush victim, establish IV fluids if possible. (3) Monitor for hyperkalemia and renal failure following extraction. (4) Treat for hypothermia as trapped victims lose body heat rapidly. (5) Immobilize all suspected spinal injuries. (6) Apply tourniquets for uncontrollable limb bleeding during extraction. (7) Transport critical patients to trauma centers with surgical capability.

metadata.documentTitle: NDMA Guidelines on Fire Emergency Management
metadata.cleanText: Fire prevention measures include: (1) Ensuring all buildings comply with National Building Code fire safety norms. (2) Installing fire detection and alarm systems in commercial and high-rise buildings. (3) Maintaining adequate fire exits, staircases, and escape routes. (4) Conducting regular fire safety audits and drills. (5) Ensuring availability of fire extinguishers and fire hydrants. (6) Restricting storage of flammable materials in residential areas. (7) Proper electrical wiring inspection and maintenance. (8) Installing lightning arrestors in buildings over 15 meters height.

metadata.documentTitle: NDMA Guidelines on Fire Emergency Management
metadata.cleanText: During a fire emergency: (1) Immediately call the fire services emergency number 101. (2) Activate building fire alarm and begin evacuation. (3) Use stairways, never elevators, during fire evacuation. (4) Crawl low under smoke to breathe cleaner air near the floor. (5) Feel doors before opening — hot doors indicate fire on the other side. (6) If trapped, close doors between you and the fire, seal gaps with wet cloth. (7) Signal for help from a window using a flashlight or bright cloth. (8) Fire services personnel should establish water supply, deploy aerial ladder platforms for high-rise rescues, and conduct systematic floor-by-floor search.

metadata.sectionTitle: First Aid for Fire Burn Injuries
metadata.cleanText: For burn injuries: (1) Remove the person from the fire source and ensure scene safety. (2) Cool the burn immediately with clean, cool running water for at least 20 minutes. (3) Do not apply ice, butter, toothpaste, or any home remedy to burns. (4) Remove clothing and jewelry near the burn unless stuck to the skin. (5) Cover the burn loosely with a sterile or clean bandage. (6) For severe burns covering large body areas, wrap the person in a clean sheet. (7) Monitor for signs of shock: pale skin, weakness, rapid pulse. (8) Seek immediate medical attention for burns affecting the face, hands, feet, genitals, or that cover large areas.

metadata.documentTitle: NDMA Guidelines on Management of Floods
metadata.cleanText: Flood preparedness involves early warning systems, community awareness programs, and pre-positioning of relief materials. Key measures include: (1) Establishing flood forecasting and warning systems through the Central Water Commission. (2) Preparing flood plain zoning maps to identify vulnerable areas. (3) Building raised platforms and flood shelters in flood-prone areas. (4) Stocking essential relief materials including food, drinking water, medicines, and rescue equipment. (5) Training community volunteers in search and rescue operations. (6) Ensuring availability of boats and life jackets in vulnerable zones.

(5) Training community volunteers in search and rescue operations. (6) Ensuring availability of boats and life jackets in vulnerable zones.

metadata.documentTitle: NDMA Guidelines on Management of Floods
metadata.cleanText: During a flood emergency: (1) Activate District and State Emergency Operations Centers. (2) Issue evacuation orders for low-lying and flood-prone areas. (3) Deploy NDRF and SDRF teams for search and rescue operations. (4) Establish relief camps with adequate provisions for food, water, sanitation, and medical care. (5) Coordinate with Indian Army, Navy, and Air Force for aerial rescue operations when required. (6) Set up communication networks using satellite phones and ham radios. (7) Ensure continuous monitoring of river gauge levels and dam discharge data. (8) Provide medical teams at relief camps for treating waterborne diseases.

metadata.documentTitle: NDMA Guidelines on Management of Floods
metadata.cleanText: Citizens should: (1) Move to higher ground immediately when flood warnings are issued. (2) Avoid walking or driving through floodwaters — six inches of moving water can knock you down. (3) Stay away from power lines and electrical wires during flooding. (4) Store drinking water in clean containers as water supply may become contaminated. (5) Keep important documents in waterproof bags. (6) Follow instructions from local authorities and emergency services. (7) Do not attempt to cross swollen rivers or streams. (8) After floodwaters recede, check for structural damage before re-entering buildings.

metadata.documentTitle: NDRF Standard Operating Procedures for Disaster Response
metadata.cleanText: NDRF battalions are pre-positioned based on vulnerability assessment: (1) Each NDRF battalion comprises 1,149 personnel organized into specialist teams. (2) Teams include medical first responders, engineers, dog squads, and deep divers. (3) Pre-positioning occurs 24-48 hours before anticipated disaster based on IMD advisories. (4) Each team carries self-contained equipment including inflatable boats, chainsaws, hydraulic cutters, pneumatic tools, and communication equipment. (5) State authorities requisition NDRF through the National Emergency Response Centre. (6) Teams maintain 2-hour mobilization readiness at all times.

metadata.documentTitle: NDRF Standard Operating Procedures for Disaster Response
metadata.cleanText: Search and rescue operations follow standardized protocols: (1) Establish Incident Command System with clearly defined roles. (2) Conduct primary search for surface victims and walking wounded. (3) Use specialized equipment for confined space rescue: seismic listening devices, fiber optic cameras, concrete cutters. (4) Deploy canine search teams for locating trapped survivors. (5) Establish medical triage at rescue site. (6) Maintain detailed records of all rescued, injured, and deceased persons. (7) Coordinate with local hospitals for patient transfer. (8) Establish communication with affected families through information centers.

metadata.documentTitle: NDRF Standard Operating Procedures for Disaster Response
metadata.cleanText: Evacuation procedures: (1) Identify evacuation routes and alternate routes in advance. (2) Designate assembly points and relief camp locations. (3) Prioritize evacuation of vulnerable populations: elderly, children, disabled, pregnant women. (4) Use boats, helicopters, and military vehicles for evacuation from inundated areas. (5) Maintain evacuation roster with names, ID numbers, and destination. (6) Ensure relief camps have adequate water supply (minimum 15 liters per person per day), food, sanitation, and medical facilities. (7) Register all evacuees and maintain family reunification records.

metadata.documentTitle: WHO Guidelines on Basic First Aid in Emergency Settings
metadata.cleanText: In mass casualty incidents, use START (Simple Triage and Rapid Treatment) triage: (1) Walking wounded are GREEN (minor) — direct to treatment area. (2) Check breathing: if not breathing after repositioning airway, tag BLACK (deceased). (3) If breathing rate is over 30/minute, tag RED (immediate). (4) Check perfusion using capillary refill: if over 2 seconds, tag RED (immediate). (5) Check mental status: if patient cannot follow simple commands, tag RED (immediate). (6) Otherwise, tag YELLOW (delayed). Triage tags should be clearly visible and include patient number, time, vital signs, and treatments given.

metadata.documentTitle: WHO Guidelines on Basic First Aid in Emergency Settings
metadata.cleanText: To control severe bleeding: (1) Apply direct pressure to the wound using a clean cloth or bandage. (2) If blood soaks through, add more cloth on top — do not remove the original dressing. (3) Elevate the injured limb above heart level if possible. (4) For life-threatening limb bleeding uncontrolled by direct pressure, apply a tourniquet 5-7 cm above the wound. (5) Note the time of tourniquet application. (6) Keep the patient warm and lying down to prevent shock. (7) Seek immediate medical help. (8) Monitor vital signs continuously until emergency medical services arrive.

metadata.documentTitle: WHO Guidelines on Basic First Aid in Emergency Settings
metadata.cleanText: For drowning victims: (1) Ensure your own safety before attempting rescue — use reach, throw, row, go method. (2) Remove the person from water and place on a firm, flat surface. (3) Check for responsiveness and breathing. (4) If not breathing, begin CPR immediately: 30 chest compressions followed by 2 rescue breaths. (5) Continue CPR until emergency medical services arrive or the person starts breathing. (6) If the person vomits, turn them on their side to prevent choking. (7) Remove wet clothing and cover with dry blankets to prevent hypothermia. (8) All drowning victims should be evaluated at a hospital even if they appear to recover.

metadata.documentTitle: NDMA Guidelines on Management of Earthquakes
metadata.cleanText: Earthquake preparedness includes: (1) All buildings in seismic zones III, IV, and V must comply with Bureau of Indian Standards IS 1893 earthquake-resistant design codes. (2) Conduct seismic vulnerability assessments and retrofit critical infrastructure. (3) Prepare family earthquake emergency kits with water, food, first aid, flashlight, and battery-powered radio. (4) Identify safe spots in every room: under sturdy tables, desks, or against interior walls. (5) Secure heavy furniture, water heaters, and gas appliances to walls. (6) Know how to shut off gas, electricity, and water supply. (7) Practice Drop, Cover, Hold On drills regularly.

metadata.documentTitle: NDMA Guidelines on Management of Earthquakes
metadata.cleanText: During an earthquake: (1) If indoors, Drop to the ground, take Cover under a sturdy desk or table, and Hold On until shaking stops. (2) Stay away from windows, exterior walls, and anything that could fall. (3) If outdoors, move to a clear area away from buildings, power lines, and trees. (4) If driving, pull over to the side of the road and stop; stay inside the vehicle. (5) After shaking stops, evacuate damaged buildings and move to designated open assembly areas. (6) Be prepared for aftershocks. (7) Check for injuries and provide first aid. (8) Do not use elevators. (9) NDRF teams should conduct systematic search and rescue using specialized equipment including seismic listening devices, rescue cameras, and pneumatic lifting equipment.

metadata.documentTitle: NDMA Guidelines on Management of Earthquakes
metadata.cleanText: After an earthquake: (1) Do not enter visibly damaged buildings until structural engineers have assessed safety. (2) Check for gas leaks — if you smell gas, open windows and leave immediately. (3) Inspect foundations, walls, and chimneys for cracks. (4) Watch for fallen power lines and report them to the electricity department. (5) Buildings with structural damage should be marked with red, yellow, or green tags indicating unsafe, restricted use, or inspected conditions. (6) Document all damage with photographs for insurance and relief claims.

metadata.documentTitle: NDMA Guidelines on Management of Cyclones
metadata.cleanText: India Meteorological Department issues cyclone warnings in four stages: (1) Pre-Cyclone Watch — 72 hours before expected landfall. (2) Cyclone Alert — 48 hours prior, issued to specific coastal districts. (3) Cyclone Warning — 24 hours prior, with expected wind speed and storm surge. (4) Post-Landfall Outlook — continued tracking after landfall. Preparedness includes strengthening roofs, storing water and food supplies for 72 hours, securing loose objects outdoors, identifying nearest cyclone shelter locations, and trimming tree branches that could damage structures.

metadata.documentTitle: NDMA Guidelines on Management of Cyclones
metadata.cleanText: During cyclone: (1) Move to designated cyclone shelters or pucca buildings. (2) Stay indoors away from windows. (3) If the eye of the cyclone passes over, remain sheltered — the storm will resume from the opposite direction. (4) Disconnect electrical appliances. (5) Keep battery-powered radio for weather updates. (6) After the cyclone, stay away from downed power lines, damaged buildings, and floodwaters. (7) NDRF deploys pre-positioned teams with inflatable boats, tree cutters, and communication equipment for rescue and relief operations in the affected coastal zones.
